Hon MAURICE WILLIAMSON (Ministe r for Building and Construction)  on
behalf of the Minister of Justice: I move, That, pursuant to secti on 4D of the Electoral
Act 1993 and section 32 of the Crown Entities Act 2004, this House recommend His
Excellency the Governor-General appoint Ja ne Christine Huria as a member and the
Deputy Chair of the Electoral Co mmission for a term of four years.  The Electoral
(Administration) Amendment Act 2010, passed by this House in May of 2010,
established a new Electoral Comm
ission that took on the functions of both the former
commission and the Chief Electoral Of ficer. The Electoral (Administration)
Amendment Bill (No 2), currently before th is House, proposes transferring further
19704 Appointments 23 Jun 2011
functions to the commission, namely those of the Chief Registrar of Electors, from
2012. This will complete the amalgamation of electoral administration from three
separate agencies into but one. The Elect oral Commission is an  independent Crown
entity governed by three members. On 24 August 2010 the Governor-General appointed
the Hon Justice Hugh Williams QC as the ch air of the commission for 3 years, and Mr
Robert Peden as the Chief Electoral Officer and the chief executive of the commission
for a term of 5 years. The deputy chair position was and has remained vacant while a
candidate, with the support of the House, was being identified.
Today I am pleased to move the appointment of Jane Christine H ūria as the Deputy
Chair of the Electoral Commission. I am conf ident she will be a strong member of the
commission and will bring a variety of co mplementary skills and experiences to the
role. Mrs H ūria is a professional company director and is a director and shareholder of
HSR Governance Ltd, a company that specialis es in governance, strategy, and review.
Her current board memberships include th e Accident Compensation Corporation, the
outgoing Legal Services Agency, the Red Cross 2011 Earthquake Commission, Winter
Games NZ, and the Ng āi Tahu - mandated health and soci al services broker He Oranga
Pounamu. She is also chair of  the advisory board to trus tees of the Christchurch
Earthquake Appeal Trust, a lay member of the Health Practitioners Disciplinary
Tribunal, and a mentor in the New Zeal and Olympic Committee women in governance
programme. Mrs Hūria is Ngāi Tahu, and affiliates to Ng āi Tūahuriri. I am proposing a
4-year term of appointment for Mrs H ūria under section 32(1)(b) of the Crown Entities
Act 2004. Appointments to the commission may be made for 5 years or any shorter
period stated in the notice of appointment. A 4-year term is proposed in order to phase
the members’ appointments term so that the review of this appointment does not occur
in an election year. I commend this appointment to the House.

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: The Electoral Commission has been
significantly revamped under the amendments to the Electoral Act that have been
passed by Parliament during this term. The commission has already undertaken
significant work, with the Botany by-election under its purview. It now has the carriage
of the administrative arrangements for the Te Tai Tokerau by-election, and the general
election, which is to co me before the end of the year. Then it will take on further
functions, including the work that is curren tly discharged by the Electoral Enrolment
Centre, when it takes on those functions under the legislation.
The legislation provides for three commi ssioners, but only two are currently in
office: the Hon Hugh Williams and Robert  Peden, the Chief Electoral Officer. I
remember when the Hon Hugh Williams was fi rst appointed to judicial office back in
1989. I was the law clerk to the Chief Justice at the time, and I had to write the notes for
the speech that the Chief Justice gave at the swearing-in of Mr Williams as a Master of
the High Court, as Associate Judges of the High Court were then known. It is significant
that although it is no longer a requirement of the Act th at a judge act as Chair of the
Electoral Commission, the House has chosen to recommend to the Governor-General
that that tradition continue in this transition al period, as the new commission establishes
itself.
It is also significant to note, because it will  relate to a couple of comments that I am
going to make in conclusion, that the Hon Hugh Williams not only has judicial
experience, and therefore, as we would all hope, will bring an impartial approach to the
very important position of Chair of the El ectoral Commission, but also has significant
governance experience in his own right. I reca ll that prior to his appointment as a
Master of the High Court, he served as president of what was then the Manawat ū
District Law Society, and immedi ately prior to taking judicial office, he also served a
23 Jun 2011 Appointments 19705
term as president of the New Zealand Law Society. After he was appointed as a full
judge of the High Court, he also served a 6-year term as chan cellor of the Massey
University Council. So in those roles he learnt at the coalface, if you like, wh at it is like
to have to govern an organisation. What I hope we are seeing here is a transition from
the tradition of having to have judges sitti ng as the head of the body that runs elections
and matters associated with elections to recognising that  although we need impartial
people on the Electoral Commi ssion, it is equally vital to have people with governance
experience, particularly given the expans ion of the role of the commission—the
merging of the three electoral agencies—that the House has determined ought to occur.
The other current commissioner, as I mentioned, is Robert Peden, the Chief Electoral
Officer. Mr Peden was formerly the chief le gal adviser to the Electoral Commission,
prior to taking on the role as Chief Electora l Officer. I do not think there would be
anybody in the House who would question Mr Peden’s commitment to independence or
to fearlessly policing the rigours of the electoral law, as it has been enacted.
I want to say one or two other things about the legislation as it now stands. It is
instructive to compare section 8 of the Electoral Act 1993 with se ction 4D. Section 8
was the old appointments section, now repealed. Section 4D is the new one. Section 8
required, as I said, that there be a judge appointed to the Electoral Commission. It could
be a judge at various levels  of the system, but it was almost invariably a High Court
judge. The appointment had to occur from —if a High Court judge—three candidates
offered by the head of bench, the Chief Justic e, for that purpose. So Parliament was
very restricted in its choices as to who might head th e commission. The Secretary for
Justice sat, as of right, on the co mmission; so did a judge of the M āori Land Court. All
those requirements have been swept aside, a nd now there is just the requirement that
there be the three commissioners. I think that  is an important step forward, as I say,
given the expansion of the role of the electoral agency a nd given not only the
independence but also the governance expertise that we now expect of it.
The other significant matter in the legi slation is the enhancement of the
independence of the commission by the very words of the Act. I noted the careful words
that were in the Minister’s speech. He corr ectly pointed out that no one other than the
Governor-General appoints the members of the commission. It is also important to point
out that these appointments are not made in the usual way on the recommendation or
advice of a Minister; they are made on the recommendation of this House. In that regard
it is of concern to see the Government House website describing the Chair of the
Electoral Commission as having been nominated by the Minister of Justice. Of course,
that is not the procedure. The procedure is that the Minister circulates names around the
House to various parties, and the names that win unanimous approval are the ones that
go forward under a communication from the Minist er, but on behalf of this House. That
is a very important point, I think, just to reiterate.

items.speaker: We come to the business of the motion
items.text: the proposal to fina lly appoint a third
member of the Electoral Commission and to bring it to full strength, which is not
something that could happen too soon, given the workload that I have mentioned and
given the functions and tasks that the agency will have to fulfil over the coming months.
I am aware that there was another candida te who met the approva l of parties around
the House, and who might have been appoint ed to fill the deputy chair’s position and
thereby bring the com
mission to full strengt h, but that person, although eminently
qualified, has elected to perform paid wo rk for the commission in its education
campaign on the referendum, which is to occur at the end of the year. So that person’s
skills are being utilised by the commission, but not in a governance role.
19706 Appointments 23 Jun 2011
It is clear from Ms H ūria’s curriculum vitae that she has significant governance
skills, so to that extent he r appointment as deputy chair is to be welcomed. The only
note of caution that I would sound on behalf  of the Opposition is that although Ms
Hūria has a very impressive CV, with respect to her, the danger, as often occurs with
people who are busy directors, is that she may have too much on. Given the recitation of
the appointments she holds that we heard fr om the Minister, and also given the busy
workload that the commission will have over the next year or so, it will be very
important that she and the ot her commissioners ensure that they have appropriate time
to devote to the important work of the commission.
Having said that, I am glad to see that th e commission is now at full strength. It is
appropriate, given the tasks that lie ahead. I wish Ms H ūria and the other members of
the commission well in the tasks that lie ah ead of them, and I am delighted to confirm
that the Labour Opposition will support this appointment.

items.speaker: SUE KEDGLEY
items.text: I likewise state that th e Green Party very much
welcomes the appointment of Ms H ūria as a member and the Deputy Chair of the
Electoral Commission. As the previous speaker, Charles Chauvel, has indicated, there is
a huge task for the Electoral Commission over the next few years overseeing the
referendum and a second referendum. We too are relieved that we now have full
membership on the Electoral Commission.
We are impressed by the curriculum vitae of Ms H ūria. We agree that it looks as
though she is extremely productive. We hope th at she is not stretched in too many
directions, because the Electoral Commission will need a great deal of focus, effort, and
attention to steer successfully through the next period of referendums on MMP, etc. We
affirm our support for this appointment.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Deputy
Speaker. Thank you for the opportunity to have  a say about the a ppointment of Jane
Hūria as deputy chair of the Electoral Commission. The M āori Party stands to support
Jane’s appointment to that position. In doing so, we firstly mihi to Ng āi Tahu and Ng āi
Tūahuriri on the honour of this appointme nt—an appointment that we believe is
absolutely warranted.
It is a particularly interesting day for this appointment to come before the House.
Jane is a member of the Red Cross 2011 Earthquake Commission, which has been set
up to provide charitable relief to the Christchurch community from the effects of the
recent earthquakes and aftershocks. As Christ church is no doubt still reeling from the
announcements made earlier this afternoon about properties and houses no longer able
to be lived in, we are pleased that th ere is something special at least for Ng āi Tahu to
consider in terms of the appointment of this very strong nominee.
As I understand it, and as has been expresse d in this House, Jane comes to this
position with a wealth of experience in  governance and organisation. She has broad-
based commercial experience, including in law, insurance, market research, and
financial markets. In addition to that experi ence she has directorships in the electricity,
technology, business development, educa tion, insurance, property development,
agribusiness, seafood marketing, and sport and recreation sectors.
As other speakers have said, she serves on a num
ber of boards,  and she is a lay
member of the Health Practitioners Disc iplinary Tribunal and a member of the
management advisory group for the Secretary to the Treasury. If all of that is not
enough, she is also patron of the University  of Canterbury Founda tion, a supporter of
the Christchurch Arts Festival, and a board member of the Court Theatre. Not only does
she sit on many of those boards but also sh e develops and teaches public and in-house
governance courses for the Inst itute of Directors in New Zealand, for the Tertiary
Education Commission for university, polytechnic, and wānanga councils, and for Sport
23 Jun 2011 Appointments 19707
and Recreation New Zealand. All of these quali fications make her an ideal applicant for
the position.
There is one more reason that I think it is  particularly pleasing that tangata whenua
has been appointed to this particular ro le. In the recent process of broadcasting
allocations, we believe that decisions were made that in effect devalue the role of the
Treaty and of te reo M āori as the official language of Aotearoa. The M āori Party
allocation was dramatically reduced between 2008 and 2011 to the effect of a loss of
some $90,000. We could not help but wonder whether confusion has arisen over the
differing legislative responsibilities that govern the broadcasting allocation process—
namely, between the Broadcasting Act 1989 and the Electoral Ac t 1993. Although the
Broadcasting Act has clear requirements on promoting M āori language and M āori
culture, the Electoral Act refers only to M āori representation. We  were astounded that
the only party that exclusively represents the Māori electorates was allocated less than 5
percent of the funding for a population that represents 17 percent of the New Zealand
population.
We hope, therefore, that this appointment will give special cap acity to speak to
tangata whenua as the Treaty partner, to focus on voting constituencies that have been
historically under-represented with low turn-out, particularly of young Māori, and to our
unique capacity to express our message  through te reo ra ngatira, te reo M āori. We
strongly support the appointment of Jane Hūria.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I rise to support the a ppointment of the third
Electoral Commissioner. The reason this comes to this House is that we in New Zealand
have a long tradition of well-run elections. I think we can be very, very proud of the fact
that we run non-corrupt elections in New Zealand. We have public confidence in our
election processes, which is one of the r easons why New Zealand has relatively high
rates of voter participation in  our democratic elections. Peop le know that if  they cast
their vote, it will be counted properly, and that there will not have been corrupt practices
in the electoral process, that political par ties do their utmost to comply with the laws,
and that we have independent bodies like the Electoral Commission overseeing
elections to make sure that the laws that  this country has built up over the years are
adhered to.
One of the ways we maintain the confidence of political parties across the political
divide in the process is that when we ma ke appointments to the Electoral Commission,
which oversees elections, we make sure that that process is not politicised. We do not
see the former president of the Labour Party being appointed to the Electoral
Commission, and we do not see the former  president of the National Party being
appointed to the Electoral Commission; we see independent people who are of standing
in the community who politic al parties across the House can agree are appropriate
people to oversee elections and maintain our  confidence in those processes and also,
more important, maintain broader public confidence in those processes so that we
m
aintain confidence in our democratic institutions.
There is a saying that the only thing worse th an democracy is the alternative. That is
a backhanded way of saying that democracy is very, very important. We in this House
all understand that democracy—for all its flaws,  for all its frustrations at times, and for
all its niggles and our sometimes immature behaviour in this H ouse—overall delivers
better outcomes than Saddam Hussein managed to in Iraq despite a wealth of oil money.
Despite various other despots in other pa rts of the world, democracy delivers good
outcomes.
In New Zealand we have one of the longe st unbroken democracies in the world, and
we can be very proud of that. We have strong traditions, and those traditions are, in my
opinion, almost more important than the written rules of la w. But those traditions are
19708 Appointments 23 Jun 2011
reinforced and upheld thr ough good rules of law. We in New Zealand have good
electoral law, and we try across this Parliament to agree on the structure of it. We do not
always agree. There is always disagreemen t at the margins. The Labour Party does not
think we do as well as we could on the transparency of donations, which can be made in
a way that undermines public confidence in our el ectoral processes, but we have some
pretty strict rules around what is spent on elections and where the funding for that
spending comes from, even if in some situ ations we do not have clarity as to who
donated the money.
The people we rely upon to oversee our ru les around elections are at the Electoral
Commission. That is the body th at we have formed in recent years to take over the
functions that were previous ly split between two bodies. The Electoral Commission is
already quite busy; it has had a by-election recently—the Botany by-election—since its
formation, and of course we have another this weekend, in  Te Tai Tokerau. I wish the
candidates well in that  election, and I thank them for their efforts. We rely upon the
Electoral Commission to oversee the rules to make sure that we are all playing by the
same ground rules, so that we do not descend into the sort of nonsense—and I think it is
nonsense—that we have in places like the United States of America. Enormous amounts
of money are spent on elections, enormous amounts of money are spent on lobbyists,
and the outcomes are no more just or good for their country. In fact, I would suggest
that they are less just than the outcomes we generally achieve in New Zealand.
We rely upon the members of the Electoral Commission to oversee those rules. We
already have two of those officers. The first is the Hon Hugh Williams, a former High
Court judge, who is in charge of this body; I understand he is the chair. Is that right, Mr
Chauvel? He is the chair. We also have ha d Robert Peden, the Chie f Electoral Officer,
appointed to a role on the Electoral Commission. Today’s appointment of Ms Hūria is
the third of the three appointees that are provided for under the law.
We are, of course, coming up to an el ection within 6 months. The Electoral
Commission already has the workload in respect of those by-elections I have referred to.
We are dealing with a new law, so the Elec toral Commission will be required to make a
few rulings that will be slightly different from earlier rulings, because the rules have
changed. There are some issues that relate to the dual sign-off that we will now need
between the Parliamentary Service and the Electoral Commission in respect of some
spending that is of proper parliamentary purpos e but also falls within the definition of
an election advertisement. In  respect of those perfectly legal transactions, we as
parliamentarians will have to negotiate bo th the rules relating to the Parliamentary
Service and the rules relating to the Elect oral Commission. We look forward to some
sensible rulings from both of those bodies as we parliamentarians try our best to adhere
to the rules of the law.
The attributes of Ms H ūria have been well canvassed by other speakers, and I do not
propose to repeat them. Suffice it to say that  her experience is wide ranging, and has
included public roles as well as roles for private companies. We on the Labour Party
side of the House have confiden ce that she is a suitable appoin tee to this role. I will not
say anything more than that. The Labour Party supports the appointment of Ms Hūria as
the third member of the Electoral Commission.
Motion agreed to.

Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister of Transport)  on behalf of the Attorney-

items.speaker: General
items.text: I m ove, That, pursuant to section 8A (2) of the Judicial Conduct
Commissioner and Judicial Conduct Pane l Act 2004, this House recommend His
Excellency the Governor-General appoint Mr Alan Deans Ritchie of Wellington as the
Deputy Judicial Conduct Commissioner for a term of five years from the date of
23 Jun 2011 Appointments 19709
appointment having noted that the Attorney-General advises this House, in accordance
with section 8A(3) of the Act, that the Chief Justice has been consulted about the
proposed appointment. The Judicial Conduct Commissioner and Judicial Conduct Panel
Act 2004 came into effect on 1 August 2005.  The role of deputy commissioner was
established by section 8A of the Act as recently amended. The Act provides for the
Office of the Judicial Conduct Commissioner and sets out a statutory regime for dealing
with complaints about judges’  conduct. If appropriate the commissioner or the deputy
commissioner may recommend the appointment of a judicial conduc t panel to inquire
into any matter about the conduct of a judge.
The Act established processes that recognise  and protect the requirement of judicial
independence and natural justice. The deputy commissioner will perform the
commissioner’s functions when the commi ssioner has a conflict of interest or is
otherwise unavailable to address a complaint.  In performing thes e functions the deputy
commissioner will be required to act independently.
The Attorney-General has received support from all parties for the appointment of
Mr Alan Ritchie as the Deputy Judici al Conduct Commissioner. Mr Ritchie was
admitted as a barrister and solicitor in 1971. He  practised with Spen cer and Ritchie in
Ashburton and Chapman Tripp in Wellington  for some 12 years. He has been a
consultant to the New Zealand Law Society since 2008 and was the chief executive
officer and executive director from 1985 to  2008. He is also a member of the New
Zealand Parole Board. In 2008 Mr Ritchie spent 3 to 4 months deputising for the
previous Judicial Conduct Commissioner. The term of appointment must be for not less
than 2 years and not more than 5. It is pr oposed that Mr Ritchie be appointed for 5
years. The deputy commissioner is remunera ted at a rate set by the Remuneration
Authority and the current commissioner is Sir David Gascoigne.

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: Although it is always a pleasure to hear from Mr
Joyce, it is a shame that the Attorney-Gener al was not able to move the motion we have
just heard, because it would have been too difficult to resist the temptation to remind the
Attorney-General of what he said when it was first proposed by the Labour Government
that the Office of the Judici al Conduct Commissioner be cr eated. He said: “The Labour

items.speaker: Party approach is illustrated by this foolish legislation
items.text: set up an office, create
procedures, appoint a commissioner, and then bring on the inevitable amendment bill
that seeks to appoint a deputy commissioner. ” Well, he was quite right, except, of
course, that an amendment bi ll came in under the National Government last year. “The
next thing we will have is a registrar, a council of worthies, hundreds of bureaucrats,
and, lo and behold, a culture of complaint being encouraged and nurtured. There are
plenty of litigants out there who, having lo st their cases, will personalise them against
judges. They are encouraged by this ridiculous regime to make complaints.” I suppose it
is different being in Government, as we saw with the flip-flop over the therapeutic
goods administration earlier in the week.
Turning to the merits of the motion, I tell members that new sections 8A and 8B of
the Judicial Conduct Commissioner and Judi cial Conduct Panel Act 2004 now provide
for an office called the Deputy Judicial Conduct Commissioner, and I remember the
debates we had in the House on this last y ear. The reality is that the Judicial Conduct
Commissioner has become an important office. It is a place where people feel that they
can go when they have a concern about the way they have been treated in our court
system that they do not like. As a result, the number of people seeking to use the office
has increased greatly.
I looked at the annual report of the Judici al Conduct Commissioner from last year,
where Sir David Gascoigne ta kes great care to recoun t the level and volume of
complaints that have been made to his office.  It is instru ctive to consider that report,
because it indicates that not only have peopl e found the office to be a useful place to
19710 Appointments 23 Jun 2011
take concerns and complaints but also the number of complaints that have been found to
have any substance is very, very small. So I think we can take double comfort from this.
First, people are using the office—hence the need for a deputy to the Judicial Conduct
Commissioner. But, secondly, many of the co mplaints are not being upheld. So people
have a safety valve. They have somewhere they can go if they do not feel well treated
and they get a decent process. The complaint is investigated, and, no doubt, they feel
they have had a fair hearing as a result of the process. But in the end it is confirmed that,
generally speaking, we have a judiciary that is working well, because most of the
complaints are not upheld. So there are two reasons to be pleased about the way this
office is working and the fact that it has been introduced.
The other comment that is useful to not e in the report of the Judicial Conduct
Commissioner is that the judiciary itself has been very cooperative with the Office of
the Judicial Conduct Commissioner. Judges are independent: they have tenure, they are
not public servants, and they are under no dut y to cooperate with any statutory officer
whom we may appoint. The fact that they ha ve almost universally adopted an approach
that is cooperative indicates that they too have come to welcome this move as one that
enhances confidence in the judicial proce ss and in our judiciary—a very important
pillar, one of the three, in our constitution. They are things that I think are appropriate to
put on record, particularly given certain events over the last year.
Mr Ritchie is somebody who is known to any lawyer who practised during the period
that he was executive director of the New Zealand Law Society. I was admitted to the
Bar in 1989; he began working at the New Zealand Law Society in 1985. All
communications from the society were signed by him, and he was a figure who I think
was regarded as somebody who worked diligently  as an administrator in the society. As
the motion from the Attorney-General on the Or der Paper records, as is required by the
Act, this is an appointment that the Chief Ju stice concurred with, so we can fully expect
that the cooperation that has been extended to  Sir David Gascoigne in his role as Chief
Judicial Conduct Commissioner will be extended  also to Alan Ritchie, as his deputy.
We can fully expect that the confidence that has been enhanced in the judiciary by the
existence of this office and its fair and full processing of complaints will also continue.
There are other things that this House needs to look forward to. One member has
already foreshadowed a proposal to bring fo rward a register of judicial pecuniary
interests, and members on this side of the House have indica ted that we approve of that
general approach and would s upport it. It is nece ssary in this day and age that every
public official appointed or elected acts with appropriate  transparency, and it is
inevitable that that is the di rection in which we are moving. It is something that, rather
than running from, all actors in the consti tutional drama should actually embrace. But,
as I say, the appointment of Alan Ritchie is supported by members on this side, and we
hope that his work as the inaugural De puty Judicial Conduct Commissioner will
continue to bolster the important work that the Office of the Judicial Conduct
Commissioner conducts, in terms of assuring people that the judiciary is somewhere
they can go for a fair and full disposal of the litigation they may wish to engage in.

items.speaker: SUE KEDGLEY
items.text: The Green Party also supports and welcomes the
appointment of Mr Alan Ritchie as Deputy Judicial Conduct Commissioner. He has had
a very distinguished—indeed, exemplary—legal  career, and I think he is very well
suited to this new role.
I agree with the previous speaker, Charle s Chauvel, that although the Office of the
Judicial Conduct Commissioner is reasonably new, it has establis hed itself as an
important place of last resort that people can go to when they feel aggrieved by the court

23 Jun 2011 Appointments 19711
pleased that this body exists, and that people, as I said, have a place of last resort where

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I rise to take a brief ca ll also in s upport of this
appointment. Alan Ritchie is well-known to most members of the legal community in

Mr Ritchie had a similar role to that when he was at the New Zealand Law Society
for many years and was secretary of the New Zealand Law Society, I think—

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to
speak on this very important Smoke-free Environment (Controls and Enforcement)
Amendment Bill. This bill imposes cont rols on the marketing, advertising, and
promotion of tobacco products, and it is another significant step forward in reducing the
19712 Smoke-free Environments Amdt Bill 23 Jun 2011
harm from tobacco products here in New Zealand. The Health Committee heard 150
submissions, and the committee was in unanimity  that the measures taken in this bill
were quite appropriate.
I am sorry to see that Iain Lees-Galloway has just entered the House too late to finish
off his speech, but he made a very useful contribution during the select committee
process, and I am sure he will do in the Co mmittee stage as well. I also congratulate the
Hon Tariana Turia and the M āori Party on their consistent approach to tobacco control,
and I acknowledge the work of the M āori Affairs Committee durin g its inquiry into the
tobacco industry in Aotearoa, and its consequences for Māori. They would have liked to
see even firmer measures than are in the bill, but I do believe that the measures taken
through this amendment bill are a very important step forward in reducing harm.
I think it is also important to acknowledge  that many individuals have been involved
in the history of getting New Zealand to the pl ace where it is at now. If one thinks back
prior to the Smoke-free Environments Ac t of 1990, and even 12 to 15 years ago, one
could go into public places that were filled with smoke, such as aeroplanes, railcars, and
cafes. Most New Zealanders regard it as abso lutely wonderful that we have the option
of a clean environment.
It is important to remind the House that  there are something like 5,000 premature
deaths per year from direct smoking a nd something like 500 deaths from indirect
smoking, or second-hand smoke inhalation. There still remains a major problem in New
Zealand with smoking. As the honourable Tari ana Turia pointed out the other night,
something like 45 percent of the M āori population aged between 16 and 65 still smoke,
and something like 50 percent of young Māori women are still smoking.
There is a relentless effort by the tobacco industry to sell tobacco by whatever means
it can possibly conjure up. There have been a va riety of measures put together in this
bill to curtail the marketing, the advertisi ng, and the promotion of tobacco products. It
also includes herbal smoking products, which had not had the regulations of the Smoke-
free Environments Act enforced previously. It is very much the intention of the Health
Committee that those regulations are imposed into the future. There was some debate in
the committee as to whether some of the new synthetic products, th e cannabinoids such
as Kronic, would also fall within the measur es taken by this new legislation. However,
the view 2 or 3 months ago was that b ecause there had been no public debate or
submissions around that, that at this stage that aspect would come at a later date. I think
the force of view around the c ountry now, however, is that it  would be right and proper
to ensure that substances like Kronic, synt hetic cannabinoids, and the whole variety of
them do fall under legislation such as this as soon as possible.
Transition arrangements have been made to ensure that retailers have a reasonable
time to prepare. This Government and the se lect committee very much realise that costs
are involved, and consequently appropriate  transition arrangements have been made.
This bill does affect internet sales, and that  is right and proper, and, of course, includes
very strong penalties for tryi ng to sell products over the inte rnet to people under 18. It
also affects covert sponsorship. Here ag ain the idea is to counter the exclusive
availability of a single tobacco brand at  an event, including tobacco companies
employing people to work at events weari ng the brand’s colours. Amendments are
appropriately introduced, with some pre tty stiff penalties of up to $50,000 for a
manufacturer, importer, or distributor who breaches the bans. The penalty regime is
indeed increased. There has been great concern that in some of the minor retail stores
around New Zealand sometimes it is not the owner of the business who has had the
penalty brought against them, but that will be included in the new regime.
All in all, this is yet another step forwar d to reduce tobacco harm in New Zealand. It
is a very realistic step, and a practical step. It comes on the back of previous efforts over
23 Jun 2011 Smoke-free Environments Amdt Billl 19713
several decades, including last year a three-step imposition of a tobacco tax of 10
percent a year over 3 years. Cumulatively this is a practical, pragmatic, and important
step forward, and I look forward to the Co mmittee stage. I commend the bill to the
House.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Thank you for giving me the opportunity to
speak on the Smoke-free Environments (Cont rols and Enforcement) Amendment Bill.
This is one of the first issues that I have dealt with as a new member of the Health
Committee, and I would like to echo the co mments made by the chair of the Health
Committee, Dr Paul Hutchison, that it was a pleasure to deal with the bill in a
unanimous way. As the committee went thr ough the submissions, it acted as one and
with a unified voice, and with unified questioning, as well. It was a pleasure to be on the
committee. Of the 150 submitters on the bill, it is fair to say some inspired me, some
really annoyed me, and some outright disguste d me with some of the stuff that they
came to the committee with, in terms of what they said about this bill.
With 700,000 Kiwis smoking at this stage, I think it is pretty cl ear that smoking in
New Zealand causes significant social impacts in terms of people’s health. Labour
supports this bill because our position is to encourage New Zealand to be smoke-free by
2025. I want to paint a bit of a Pacific picture here, if I can. Some Ministry of Health
figures from 2008 show that the New Zealand average for male smoking was around the
26 percent mark, and for Pacific Island ma les it was around the 35 percent mark. For
females the reading was not much better: on average, around 22 percent of females were
smoking, but for Pacific Isla nd females the smoking rate was around the 28 percent
mark. So Pacific Islanders are disproportionately represented in the smoking statistics in
New Zealand. It is well recognised that smoking is  either a risk factor for, or a cause of,
cancers, respiratory diseases, and cardiovascul ar diseases. Some research from Action
on Smoking and Health (ASH) in 2008 also  showed that in the Pacific Island
community there were 30 deaths from can cer, about 102 deaths from cardiovascular
disease, and 23 deaths from strokes. Smoking, in terms of the Pacific Island community,
is obviously a very significant issue, but the community is dealing with it.
Smoking is also an issue within my own culture. The ASH study in 2008 showed that
42 percent of Tokelauans registered themselves as smokers, which was by far and away
the largest percentage in a Pacific grouping in New Zealand. I congratulate the
Tokelauan health community. They have recogn ised that this is a large problem within
their people, and they are taking strong steps to  try to counter that, and to ensure that
members of the Tokelauan community are quitting smoking as much as they can.
I will go back to the submissions made during the select comm ittee process. I will
congratulate a number of Pacific organisations that submitted to the select committee. In
particular, I point out one organisation th at the select committee heard from in
Auckland, I think, which was Tala Pasifika. Its programme manager, Stephanie Erick,
basically said the thrust of this bill was on the money, and that “Addressing the issues of
tobacco accessibility to youth and at-risk populations in Ne w Zealand is a major step
towards protecting current and future gene rations who would have otherwise been
vulnerable to the deadly and addictive toba cco products that currently enjoy promotion
in retail settings across the country.” She also went on to  say “To protect our Pacific
children and the wider community from bei ng initiated into smoking, the removal of
tobacco retail displays from sight is an esse ntial and urgent requirement.” I congratulate
Tala Pasifika on making that submission to the select committee, and I acknowledge the
important role that Pacific health practitioners play in making sure that they get as many
Pacific Islanders as possible to quit smoking.
19714 Smoke-free Environments Amdt Bill 23 Jun 2011
The health of the Pacific Island community is also a very topical issue today, because
this morning out on the forecourt of Parlia ment there was a 200-strong protest, I will
call it, of people from the Pacific communities of my own electorate of Mana—
predominantly from Porirua East. They came to Parliament to protest against cuts in the
health budget. I point out that it was commenda ble that the Minister  of Pacific Island
Affairs, Georgina te Heuhe u, addressed the group of pe ople that formed on the
forecourt, but it was a bit on the nose that she called it a celebration of Pacific health. It
was not that, at all. It was a hīkoi, and it was a protest. It was a hīkoi and a protest, and I
think it was a bit on the nose for those pe ople who turned up—the 200 people from my
electorate who are worried about the level of Pacific health f unding—that the Minister
of Pacific Island Affairs, although she took on board the comments and the petition
from the 200-strong protest, called that prot est a celebration. It was nothing of the sort;
it was a protest at the Government’s cut to funding in the Pacific health sector.
One of those services, Pacific Health Se rvice Porirua, has a very strong smoking
cessation programme. It is very concerned a bout what the cuts to the health budget will
do to that programme. It is not the only Pacific health prov ider in Porirua that has a
strong smoking cessation progra mme. I guess I am trying to sa y it is great to have the
will to try to make New Zealand smoke-free by 2025, but if we are to achieve that goal
we have to back up that commitment with  funding. In the communities where it will
make a big difference—and I mentioned be fore the overrepresentation of Pacific
Islanders in the smoking stat istics—we have to back up the commitment we make in
legislation with the resources to make sure that if we want to get people from the Pacific
Island communities to quit smoking, we have  people in those communities who can
encourage that.
I will turn back to some of the other issues raised at the select committee. Another
submitter—a tobacconist, I believe he was, from Dunedin; I will not mention his
name—claimed that 95 percent of his sales came from tobacco. That is obviously the
case. He claimed that he sold $150,000 worth of  cigarettes or tobacco per week through
his store in Dunedin. He basically claimed that most of his customers became friends,
and he had been selling to them for decades. I asked him during the hearing, given that
he said he had been selling to these “fri ends” for decades, how many of those people,
those customers, he believed would want to qu it. I think, if I recall correctly, he said it
would be about 70 percent. I th ink that although we are passi ng this legislation, there is
also a bit of an onus on re tailers, too. Although  New Zealanders have the freedom to
buy tobacco whenever they like if they are of the right age, there is a responsibility upon
retailers to make sure that they are doing the socially right thing, and not necessarily
feeding the habits of the people who buy tobacco from them. In that case, someone who
is selling $150,000 worth of tobacco per week  over his counter through his store, and
who thinks that about 70 percent of his cu stomers want to quit, might need to think
about some of the social responsibility that he has, too.
I will pick up on some of the earlier comm ents that Dr Paul Hutchison made, too,
about some of the details re lating to herbal products. I think it is good that the same
restrictions on herbal smoking products will come into this legislation. The same
restrictions that apply to tobacco sales will be placed on he rbal products. Also, the fines
regime is to increase for both tobacco and herbal products. I belie ve that the maximum
fine for a proprietor for selling to someone who is under age will now increase to
$10,000. I think that is a positive move, in terms of trying to make sure that we crack
down on retailers who c ontinually flout the rules and sell  cigarettes to those who are
under 18 years of age.
I finish by saying we welcome and support this bill. It was a pleasure to be on the
select committee. As I said, it was one of my first issues to deal with on the select
23 Jun 2011 Smoke-free Environments Amdt Billl 19715
committee. To sit on that committee and work on a bill such as this, which had
unanimous support from all parties, was a pl easure. I also commend  the Minister in
charge of this bill, the Hon Tariana Turia, for her work to make sure that action was
taken on this issue. The last Labour Government took some real steps, the first marker
steps, to make sure that we make New Zealand smoke-free by 2025. The Minister needs
to be commended for her efforts to make sure that the Government made this legislation
a priority, even though it took some time for National to do so. The Minister pushed it
as hard as she could, and it is a pleasure that the bill is at this stage in the House. Thank
you very much for the opportunity to speak.

items.speaker: KEVIN HAGUE
items.text: It is a pleasure to stand in support of the Smoke-free
Environments (Controls and Enforcement) Am endment Bill. I think it is one of those
occasions where—I am not sure about th e ACT Party—pretty much everyone in the
House is likely to be voting for a bill. Indeed, we may well all be giving more or less the
same speech in this debate.
I commence in that tradition by joining other speakers in expressing our appreciation
of the work undertaken by offici als from the Ministry of Hea lth in assisting the Health
Committee in its work on the bill. This is a complex area of legislation, surprisingly, but
the officials were diligent and provided good quality advice, I felt, to the select
committee. I also acknowledge the good heart and spirit with which the committee
considered the bill. As others have menti oned, the distinctions between the parties on
the Health Committee on this issue would not have been obvious to anyone coming into
the room, because the members of the commit tee worked as a single unit, and it was a
pleasure to be part of it.
The submitters were an interesting bunch. I will comment about them in a moment.
There is one person I will single out for some praise at this point in my remarks, and
that is Iain Lees-Galloway. I single him out  not for his role on the Health Committee,
but for having advanced to this House in th e first place his member’s bill to ban the
retail display of tobacco and tobacco products, which was drawn in the ballot. I suspect
that that may well have been the spur that brought this bill to the House, and I commend
Mr Lees-Galloway for that.
As I said, the submitters were an interesting bunch. I think it would be fair to say
that broadly speaking, with very few excepti ons, the submitters said that they supported
the legislation or supported its general thrust. From that point, they broke down into two
broad categories. The first of those was a cat egory of submitters who said that, yes, of
course they support the goal of New Zeala nd being a smoke-free country, and, yes, of
course they support the broad thrust of this legislation, but there are some really specific
reasons why the time frame in this bill will no t work for their particular organisation or
business, or why the particular way that the bill applies its restrictions to retail displays
will not quite work for them, and therefore they should be exempted from it. I
particularly recall an example from a submitter on behalf of the duty-free retailers at
Auckland Airport who said that although th ey were broadly supportive of this
legislation, it could not apply to duty-free retailers because of the inconvenience that
that would cause to travellers, and because th e efficiency of airpor t operations required
that passengers were able to make their duty-free purchases as quickly as possible.
Covering up the displays of tobacco products  and requiring a further step of uncovering
those tobacco products in order for passengers to be able to make their purchases would
impede the efficient operation of airports. I did not have a lo t of time for that argument,
or, indeed, for the other flimsy excuses that were advanced by the submitters in that
group. I am very pleased that the select committee resisted any temptation that may
have existed to succumb to such arguments.
19716 Smoke-free Environments Amdt Bill 23 Jun 2011
There has been a small compromise made on the commencement of the measures. I
think that was a sensible change to make, but that in itself wa s counterbalanced by
another change that the committee made, which was to greatly increase the fines. Some
other speakers have already spoken about that.
The other broad category of submitters that I would refer to are submitters like
Action on Smoking and Health, the Smokefree Coa lition, and some of those others that
Kris Faafoi, for example, just spoke about in his contribution. Those people were
excited about the fact that Parliament was taking this step. They were very strongly
supportive of the goal of a smoke-free nation, and of concrete steps being taken towards
that goal. Those submitters in general were saying that what this bill does is fantastic,
but there are other things that the bill could also do at this time. For example, they spoke
about the need for a register. One of the prac tical problems that is being encountered by
people who are out there in the field, tr ying to enforce New Zealand’s smoke-free
environments legislation, is that it is very hard to keep track of who actually is selling
tobacco and tobacco products. They argued very  strongly for the need for a register of
people selling those products. They were s upported in that by the agencies—regional
councils, public health provi ders, and the like—that do that  enforcement. I think the
case for a register is extremely strong, and the provision of a register would have indeed
been an extremely sensible addition to this bill . It is a matter of some  regret that we did
not take that step.
The other area that those submitters were suggesting the committee could advance in
the bill—to advance the cause of smoke-free environments legislation—was to pick up
some more of the recommendations of the Mā ori Affairs Committee. I have very
considerable sympathy for that point of  view. We were presented with a rare
opportunity of an extremely well-founde d and thorough investigation by the M āori
Affairs Committee. We know that the committ ee travelled the length and breadth of the
country. In an extremely thorough process, it heard from the tobacco industry as well as
from all of us who strongly support that goal of a smoke-free nation.
On the basis of that very thorough inquir y, which was supported by all parties, the
committee came up with a comprehensive se t of regulations—plain packaging for
tobacco products, for example. I believe that there was an opportunity to incorporate
more of the recommendations of the M āori Affairs Committee into this bill. The public
will reasonably say that, for goodness’ sake, this perfect vehicle—the Smoke-free
Environments (Controls and Enforcem ent) Amendment Bill—is going through
Parliament, so why on earth does Parliament not take this opportuni ty to advance that
programme of actions so that we can move at  a faster pace towards the goal that pretty
much everyone shares? That is a reasonable question: why on earth have we not taken
that opportunity?
I have no doubt at all that the denormalising of tobacco products that will occur as a
result of this bill being passed into law will be an extremely positive step forward. Other
speakers have referred to herbal smoking produ cts and to the changes that were made
and those that were not made. I think Paul Hutchison may need to check the officials’
report, because I am not sure that his char acterisation in his second reading speech of
what the bill does and does not do is entirel y correct. I think sellers and producers of
herbal smoking products should be on notice that the expectation of the select
committee is that at some point in the future we will consider changes in order to bring
those products in line with tobacco products.
In closing, I join others in  praising Minister Turia a nd, indeed, those other members
of the House who were involved with the inquiry by the M āori Affairs Committee: Tau
Henare, as the chair; Hone Harawira, a form er member of this House; and the other
23 Jun 2011 Smoke-free Environments Amdt Billl 19717
members of that committee. This is a good b ill. It could be better, but the Greens
certainly will be supporting it. Thank you.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. Ka nui
te mihi ki a koe i tēnei ahiahi. Today is not a bad day—today is not a bad day.
I thought I would start by ju st asking a few questions—n ot of you, Mr Assistant
Speaker Roy; I do not want to bring you into the debate. I will just check in with the
Hon Hekia Parata to see whether she has been  following the debate. I am sure she has,
because today is a good day for the M āori Party, I think. Let me  just check. If I was to
ask which party contributed to a M āori presence in the debate on the
Telecommunications (TSO, Broadband, and Other Matters) Amendment Bill, I ask what
the Hon Hekia Parata would say.

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: The Māori Party.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: OK. Right, we have one answ er from the Minister; that
gets her to Fiji. The second question is whic h party promoted the second reading of the
Smoke-free Environments (Controls and Enforcement) Amendment Bill.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: The Māori Party.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Oh no, stop it. Do not do that. Stop it. Let me ask the
Minister another question, which will take he r from Fiji to Hawaii. Who is the sponsor
of this particular bill right now?

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: Is it Te Urur—

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: No. The Minister should hurry up; I have only 10
minutes. It is Tariana—

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: Turia.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tariana Turia; that is right . The Minister is very good.
She must be Ng āti Porou; I can tell. The fourth ques tion is who is the co-leader of the
most high-profile, dynamic, effective, small, but stunningly good-looking—

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: Agile.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: —and agile political party? Who is the co-leader of that
party?

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: Dr Pita Sharples.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: He is one of them. Who is the other one?

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: Te Ururoa Flavell.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: No, he is not.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Tariana Turia.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: That is very good. I thank the Minister very much. I
have one more question for the Minister, ju st to check that she is not reading the
answers. Which party does the Hon Tarian a Turia belong to? She sponsored this
particular bill and is a part of that ot her legislation passed today, for which the M āori
Party has provided an energetic—

items.speaker: Hon Hekia Parata
items.text: The Māori Party.

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: It is the Māori Party. The Minister is the winner. That is
why she is a Minister: because she and some  of my other colleagues over there know
the importance of having the M āori Party beside them . I can see that you are grinning,
Mr Assistant Speaker Roy. You are smiling because you know that is the answer. I
thank the Minister.
I am really pleased to follow up from and commend the Hon Tariana Turia, co-leader
of the Māori Party, for the amazing, amazing—I w ill say it again—amazing efforts she
has made in terms of tobacco control, an d in paving the foundation for the health and
well-being of all tamariki in this nation. Is the Minister nodding? Yes, sh e was. I am
sure she was nodding to agree that this bill is important for all tamariki of this nation.
19718 Smoke-free Environments Amdt Bill 23 Jun 2011
On a little bit of a serious note, I say that the party’s tobacco campaign to rid our
shores of tobacco has resulted in a number of landmark milestones, a number of which
are included in the Smoke-free Environments Act.  It is a bit of a hi story tour. There are
things in the Act such as increasing the tobacco tax, and now we have the introduction
of legislation to ban displays and to keep tobacco out of sight and out of mind. The past
12 months have been the most rapid in the history of making policy on tobacco control
that this country has seen. Just over a year ago, in response to Māori Party advocacy, the
Māori Affairs Committee announced that it woul d carry out an inquiry into the tobacco
industry—in particular, into  the consequences for M āori of tobacco use. In March the
Hon Tariana Turia initiated a public cons ultation on the proposal to ban tobacco
displays in retail outlets, specifically announcing that the Government would ban retail
displays of tobacco. This policy has long been  sought by health campaigners in order to
denormalise tobacco, to help smokers quit, and to reduce the number of young people
taking up smoking.
Already these early steps are proving to  bring about success. The 2009 Tobacco Use
Survey showed that the current smoking rate for 15 to 65-year-olds has dropped to 21.8
percent. In real numbers that is abou t 60,000 fewer smokers. Of those 60,000, in real
numbers again, about 10,000 are estimated to be M āori. Those are pretty good statistics.
As I say, these are fantastic results, which demonstrate that people are starting to
recognise the serious harm that comes from smoking, and they are ba sically saying that
it is not worth it. Therefore the M āori Party is absolutely overwhelmed and privileged
by, and stunningly supportive of, this bill.
The amendment bill aims to remove tobacco displays from outlets, and to include
harsher penalties for the sale and purchase  of tobacco products to children and young
people. The bill makes it much more difficult for companies to enter into covert
sponsorship arrangements. This bill makes significant progress in achieving the M āori
Party goal of making Aotearoa a smoke-free nation by 2025.
The Māori Party is pleased and proud to suppo rt this bill right  through to the end—
which will be soon, I am sure—as part of our goal to rid smoking and cigarettes from
our nation, and to therefore have a health ier nation across the board. Today is a good
day, when the Māori Party says: “Yeah—we’ve done it!”. Kia ora tātou.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: I fully support all the
things that were said by both the previous speakers I have  heard since I came into the
House. I have noted that old expression “no man is an island”, but I have just taken the
opportunity to ask not the multi-choice questions  that Te Ururoa Flavell put but instead
a rather more direct question of my co lleagues who were in the Chamber when I
arrived. I asked them whether they had ever smoked. I was astonished to find that very
few have that and those who ha ve smoked did so very little. I am sure that Mr Assistant
Speaker Roy will not mind my saying that when  I asked him he said he had never ever
smoked and that that accounts for his fine  complexion, youthful appearance, and high
levels of energy and intellect ual capacity. We do not wish to  bring the Speaker into the
debate, so that will not be debated.
I stand as, I guess in one way, a little bit of  an oddity, in that I first smoked when I
was 11. I used to nick my mother’s cigarette s, one at a time. I progressed to getting a
job, and I started to buy my ow n cigarettes. Members can picture if they will a 19-year-
old Auchinvole in New Zealand, gazing with adm iration as he watched the classic Kiwi
roll his own cigarette with one hand, put it in  his mouth, light the match with one hand,
and take a puff. Eventually I perfected that art. I was mostly in the rural sector and I
perfected that art of rolling my own cigarette, sticking it in  my mouth, lighting it with a
match, and then I would take a puff and take off half my lip because the cigarette would
get stuck to my mouth.
23 Jun 2011 Smoke-free Environments Amdt Billl 19719
I remember that for social occasions when we were young bucks we used to smoke
Sobranie Black Russians. They were very, very special and very expensive cigarettes.
People like Tim Groser will remember those.  But mostly it was roll-your-owns, then
tailor-mades, and then pipes with pipe tobacco  such as Erinmore Mixture. I can smell it
now. I can smell it now.
We used to go to conferences. I was a member of the livestock improvement
movement. We had national conferences  and everybody smoked. I can remember, I
think it must have been in the 1970s, when someone moved that smoking not be
permitted during the conference. There was a stunned silence and then roars of laughter.
The next year it was put to a vote. The follo wing year it was not even mentioned; there
was just no smoking and that was that.
I used to go to political conferences. At the National Party regional conference in
Auckland my Erinmore tobacco used to be nicked by Kennedy Graham’s brother, and
we would share a good pipe of tobacco. We had a debate at the divisional meeting about
whether we should smoke. I was one of the strong proponents. I can remember using
phrases like “Have some sympathy for smokers ; they are a dying breed, and they are
dying at a faster rate than the rest of us.”  One could make quite a light-hearted speech
about that.
In the 1960s and 1970s, when I was going through adolescence, almost everybody
did smoke. If we look back at the films in those ages we see that there was an awful lot
of promotion of tobacco. I gave up when  it became more difficult to smoke. My
children have never smoked, and my wife has never smoked, although my wife has
never objected to my smoking. I have now not smoked for about 13 years because it
became harder and harder. The children would oblige me to smoke outside the house,
and they did not like me smoking in the vehicle—that sort of thing.
I still smoked my pipe—I was comfortable with it—but when a friend of mine asked
me why I smoked and started to explain, much  the way that Mr Assistant Speaker Roy
did, that it impaired one from certain functi ons compared with not smoking and that I
would have much fun in life if I did not smoke , he gave me a little bit of a challenge. I
was ordering a wrought-iron gate fro m him for my mother-in-law’s 100 th birthday, and
he could not make it in time because he was too busy. So I said “Gosh, I thought I’d
heard that you could do anything, you’re such a brilliant fellow.” And he said “So I can,
and can you stop smoking?”, so I said “Probably.” He said  “All right, you send me the
design of the gate. When you send me that, ge t rid of your pipe, all the tobacco that
you’ve saved up, cigars, and that sort of thi ng, get rid of them all, and don’t smoke ever
again, then I’ll get your gate finished.” So we did a deal. We had just moved across to
the Coast. I had a complete change of habit, lifestyle, and everything else. It was a good
time to stop.
I have never ever smoked since other than a puff of a cigarette that a colleague gave
me. I thought “No, I don’t want to go back to  that.”, and I never have. The question,
though, is what have I learnt from it? If one speaks to people and asks about their
experience of smoking, one l earns that there are not very many who have a good
experience. There are not very many peopl e who want to maintain smoking. I have
never ever had any experience with drugs, other than those administered in a hospital.
This story would perhaps be different if I had asked around about drugs. Drugs just
have not happened in my life. I have ha d no exposure and no opportunity, and I have
never sought them. So, on the one hand, I have smoked cigarettes but, on the other
hand, I have had no other drugs. People who wo rk with druggies tell me that they all
want to give up. They do not want to pers ist with them. Nicotine and other drugs like
that are very hard to kick, once they get hold of someone.
19720 Smoke-free Environments Amdt Bill 23 Jun 2011
Would I go back to smoking now? I guess if  someone produced a box of Sobranie
Black Russian cigarettes, I would give one a go. Former smokers are always vulnerable.
Alcoholics are never cured, they  tell me. Formers smokers ar e never completely cured.
It is a matter of opportunity. As I say, if someone showed me a packet of Sobranie
Black Russians or if I went into a shop a nd saw them, I might have a go. I think the
proposals in the bill to remove the visual temptation and to take away the opportunity
from people can be only a good thing.
I had the privilege of attending several sessions of the M āori Affairs Committee as it
interviewed the tobacco suppliers, which I spoke to. As a large contributor to their
fortunes, I felt entitled to have a fairly aggressive approa ch to them. I asked whether
they really stil l believed in that wonderful old ad age “cigarettes, whiskey, and wild,
wild women”. Largely, tobacco suppliers are there to generate money—profits—for
their organisation and their shareholders. Th ey will fight extraordinarily hard to
maintain that profile.
I was very supportive of the work done by the M āori Affairs Committee and was
very impressed that it almost went out on a limb and fought the issue—perhaps against
the wishes of some of their own members —but fight it the comm ittee did. I raise my
hat, of course, to the—

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: Hon Tariana Turia.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: —Hon Tariana Turia and her associates in the M āori
Party. The tobacco industry can do without  us, we can do without smoking, and we
should strive to achieve the purposes of this bill. Thank you.

items.speaker: DAVID SHEARER
items.text: I will take a very brief call on the
Smoke-free Environments (Controls and Enfo rcement) Amendment Bill. It is one of
those bills with an aspiration for New Z ealand. It aspires for New Zealand to end
smoking by 2025, which is a wonderful aspiration.
I also praise, as others have done, the work  of Tariana Turia and my colleague Iain
Lees-Galloway in pushing this bill through. As  other speakers, including Kris Faafoi,
have said, the bill builds on a lot of the work that Labour did while it was in office to
outlaw the smoking common in restaurants and bars, where it is now no longer
common.
The bill brings into force measures that I think, as others have said, will decrease
drastically the incidence of smoking. Te Urur oa Flavell talked about there being 60,000
fewer smokers, and that is a fantastic statis tic. If smoking rates continue to go down by
that amount, then that is something that we can be really proud of, and is something that
New Zealand can be happy about in terms of what this Parliament is trying to do.
The word “happy” brings me to the point Mr Flavell was talking about, in terms of
today being a happy day. It is a happy day an d we should enjoy that fact. I think he
should enjoy it too, before Saturday, which will probably be a less happy day. I was
contemplating, as he was talking with Nationa l members, my hope that voters in Te Tai
Tokerau were watching and seeing that a vote for the M āori Party is ultimately a vote
for National.
With that final remark, I commend this bill and I pledge, once again, Labour’s
support for it. Thank you.

items.speaker: CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: I am proud to say my father’s name was
Kelvin Robin Tremain. He was an All Black through the late 1950s and 1960s, and back
then was possibly, one might say, the Michae l Jones of the 1980s or the Richie McCaw
of this century. He was a member of an All Black team at a time of greats, whose names
still decorate the walls of many rugby clubs and mu seums around the world—names
such as Colin Meads, Brian Lochore, and Waka Nathan.
23 Jun 2011 Smoke-free Environments Amdt Billl 19721
The All Blacks in those days were serious smokers. I know that my father was a
smoker right throughout the period that he was an All Black. He smoked right through
his adult life. I am not proud to say this, but  in fact at his peak my dad smoked two
packets or more a day. Unfortunately, Kel di ed at 54—19 years ago. He died at 54. Can
members believe that? At 54 ye ars of age he passed away. He  died of cancer. The thing
that I want to reflect on tonight is not the fact that he died—he was a big boy; he made
his own decisions—but it is what he missed out on. What he missed out on is the last 19
years, and I just want to make quite clear the poignancy of what that means to my
family. What that means is that, yes, he knew Ange, my wife, but  he did not know my
brothers’ wives, Jan and Hetti, and he never met his 10 grandchildren. So he has never
met Sam, Will, and Lily, who are my kids. He has never met Jan’s kids, Anika, Jack,
and Greer, or Hetti’s children, Anouk, Edu, Mela, and Kully. I think that is the real loss.
I know why members on this side of th e House and around the House support this
bill so much. Yes, my dad was a big boy a nd he made his own decisions, but his life
was taken early. I totally support anything that brings about a change to the way that we
smoke in this country. This bill makes it more difficult and reduces the opportunity to
smoke. Thank you.
A party vote was called  for on the question, That the Smoke-free Environments
(Controls and Enforcement) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
Ayes 113
New Zealand National 58; New Zealand Labour 40; Green Party 8; ACT New
Zealand 1 ( Boscawen); M āori Party 3; Progressive  1; United Future 1;

items.speaker: Independent
items.text: Carter C.
Noes 4
ACT New Zealand 4 (Calvert, Douglas, Hide, Roy H).
Bill read a second time.

items.text: I seek leave for the House to rise.

items.text: Leave is sought for that purpose. Is there
anyone opposed to that course of action? There appears not to be. Leave is granted.

Child Abuse Investigations, Wellington—Multi-agency Initiative 
2. PAUL QUINN (National)  to the Minister of Police: What steps are being taken 
in the Wellington police district to improve th e investigation of child abuse and the care 
and support provided to victims? 
Hon JUDITH COLLINS (Minister of Police) : I am pleased to report that today I 
opened the country’s fourth multi-agency centr e, which will provide one-stop access to 
services for child abuse victims and improve the investigation of abuse allegations. The 
Wellington Police District accounts for about 12 percent of all child abuse 
investigations nationally, with more than 8,000 family violence reports last year. The 
new centre in Pē tone, which is called Koru House, is a joint initia tive by the police, 
Child, Youth and Family, and the Hutt Valley  District Health Board. It follows the 
establishment of similar centres in Auck land City, Counties-Manukau, and Tauranga. It 
19672 Questions for Oral Answer 23 Jun 2011 
illustrates this Government’s commitment to putting victims back at the heart of the 
justice sector. 
Paul Quinn: What services will be available at the new centre to help child abuse 
victims? 
Hon JUDITH COLLINS : The centre will provide a safe and supportive 
environment where child victims can interact  with a team of police, Child, Youth and 
Family, and health professionals. This will  include specialised medical, forensic, and 
psychological services. It will also provide a vital link from those agencies back to the 
many community groups that work so hard to provide ongoing suppor t to the victims.

Parity with Australia—GDP Per Capita 
6. Hon JOHN BOSCAWEN (Leader—ACT)  to the Minister of Finance: Has the 
gap between GDP per capita in Australia and GDP per capita in New Zealand narrowed 
or widened since his Government came to office? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associate Minister of Finance) on behalf of the Minister 
of Finance: Since the September 2008 quarter real  GDP per capita in New Zealand has 
fallen by 2.9 percent, while real GDP per capita in Australia has fallen by 0.3 percent. 
This reflects the fact that we inherited a recession from the previous Government, which 
Australia did not have, combined with Australia’s unpreceden ted minerals boom. 
However, these figures move around from year to year, and quarter to quarter, and will 
continue to do so. For example, in the fi rst quarter of this year the New Zealand 
economy looks like it has grown a little, wh ile the Australian economy has shrunk by 
1.2 percent. In the long term we believe that  sound policies and car eful and considered 
decision-making will mean that we will close this gap with Australia over time, and the 
resilience the economy has shown in recent times is a positive indicator towards that.  
Hon John Boscawen : Given that he has just acknow ledged that th e gap between 
New Zealand and Australia has widened in the last 2½ years of his administration, is it 
still a concrete goal of the Government to close the income gap with Australia by 2025; 
if not, why not? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: It is still the goal of this Government. I point out to the 
member that, as he may well be aware, the 2025 Taskforce, which was set up to 
consider how to close this gap, noted that “Y ear to year fluctuations in the income gap 
will occur, but may or may not reflect the relative merits of the policy frameworks in 
the two countries. For this reason, changes in the income gap are most accurately 
assessed over the medium term.” As I say, I refer that member to the 2025 Taskforce. 
Hon David Cunliffe : If it remains the Government’s goal to close the gap with 
Australia, how long does he think it will take to do that, and when will he give the 
public targets and milestones, given that Ne w Zealand’s GDP has fallen 3 percent since 
his Government came to power, the wage gap has widened from 30 to 35 percent of 
GDP since 2008, and a record number of New Zealanders are now voting with their feet 
and contributing to Australia’s economy, not ours? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : The member is wrong on a number of counts, as my 
colleague Mr Power referred to in relation to the numbers in the previous question. 
Also, the member persists in using befo re-tax incomes for the comparator with 
Australia, which is, again, misleading. I am surprised, actually, that the member wants 
to pop up and complain about the performan ce of the New Zealand economy, when his 
Government was responsible for the mess that we inherited at the end of 2008.
